pages.text: Weather and Climate

image.note: Cover: sun, cloud, rain and lightning over a landscape

pages.text: Contents. What Is Weather? / Where Weather Comes From / Clouds and Rain / Wind and Storms / Weather and Climate / A Changing World.

Look out of the window. Is it sunny, or grey? Warm, or cold? Still, or windy? Whatever you see, that is the weather, and it is never quite the same two days running. Weather shapes what we wear, what we do, and how we feel, and yet most of us never ask where it comes from. This is the story of the sky, and the restless air above us.

image.note: A child at a window looking at the sky

pages.text: Weather can be gentle or wild, a soft drizzle or a roaring storm. It changes hour by hour, and it is different all over the world. But behind all its moods lies one simple engine, driving every cloud and every breeze: the heat of the Sun, and the water and air of our world.

image.note: Different weathers side by side: sun, rain, storm

pages.text: Weather is simply what the air is doing, over your head, right now. Is it warm or cool? Is the air still, or moving as wind? Is it dry, or carrying water as cloud and rain? Put all of that together, at one place and time, and you have the weather.

image.note: The elements of weather: temperature, wind, rain

pages.text: And weather never sits still, because the air itself never sits still. It is always warming and cooling, rising and sinking, gathering water and letting it go. The sky above you is a vast, invisible machine, forever in motion, and its movements are the weather you feel.

image.note: The restless, moving air above the ground

pages.text: Nearly all weather begins with the Sun. The Sun warms the earth, but not evenly. It heats some places more than others, the middle of the world more than the poles, the land differently from the sea. And this uneven heating is what sets the whole sky in motion.

image.note: The Sun heating the earth unevenly

pages.text: Warm air is light, and rises. Cool air is heavier, and sinks to take its place. As warm air lifts and cool air rushes in beneath it, the air begins to move, and moving air is wind. So the Sun, simply by warming the world unevenly, stirs the whole atmosphere into life.

image.note: Warm air rising, cool air sinking and flowing in

pages.text: The Sun does something else, too. It warms the seas, the lakes, and the rivers, and lifts water from them, invisibly, into the air as a gas. This is happening all the time, all over the world: water rising quietly into the sky, more than you could ever imagine.

image.note: Water rising invisibly from the sea into the air

pages.text: High up, the air is colder, and cold air cannot hold as much water. So the rising water cools, and turns back from a gas into tiny droplets, millions upon millions of them, so small and light they float. Gathered together, those floating droplets are what we call a cloud.

image.note: Water droplets gathering into a cloud

pages.text: And when the droplets in a cloud join together, they grow heavier, until at last they are too heavy to float, and they fall. That is rain. If the air is cold enough, they fall frozen, as snow or hail. So every raindrop was once sea water, lifted by the Sun, and now returned to earth.

image.note: Droplets joining and falling as rain

pages.text: This great journey, sea to sky to cloud to rain and back to sea, goes round and round, for ever, and is called the water cycle. The very same water has been going round it for millions of years. The rain on your window may once have fallen on the dinosaurs.

image.note: The water cycle: sea, sky, cloud, rain, and back

pages.text: Wind is simply moving air, and it can be a gentle breeze or a mighty gale. Where warm air rises fast and cool air rushes in hard, the wind grows strong. Wind carries the clouds across the sky, drives the waves upon the sea, and sweeps the weather from place to place.

image.note: Wind driving clouds and waves

pages.text: Sometimes the weather turns wild. When warm, wet air rises very fast, it can build enormous storm clouds, dark and towering, crackling with lightning and booming with thunder. The greatest storms of all can spin across the sea, with winds strong enough to bend great trees. Nature, at these moments, shows its full power.

image.note: A towering storm cloud with lightning

pages.text: Lightning is a giant spark, leaping between cloud and ground, hotter than the surface of the Sun. Thunder is the sound of the air, blasted apart by that spark. You see the lightning first and hear the thunder after, because light travels faster than sound. Count the gap, and you can tell how far the storm is.

image.note: Lightning striking, thunder following

pages.text: Weather is what the sky is doing today. Climate is different. Climate is the usual weather of a place, over many, many years. One rainy day does not make a wet climate, and one hot day does not make a hot one. Climate is the pattern behind the weather, the way a place usually is.

image.note: Weather (one day) beside climate (many years)

pages.text: Different parts of the world have very different climates. Near the middle of the earth it is hot all year. Near the poles it is frozen. Some places are dry as dust, others soaked with rain. These patterns depend on how much sun a place gets, how near it is to the sea, and how high it lies.

image.note: A world map of different climates

pages.text: For a long time, the world's climates stayed much the same. But now, scientists have found that the earth as a whole is slowly growing warmer, and that this is changing weather patterns around the world. Understanding why, and caring for our world, is one of the great tasks of your time.

image.note: Scientists studying the changing climate

pages.text: So the next time rain patters on the window, or wind tugs your coat, or a storm rolls across the sky, you will know the secret engine behind it: the Sun, the water, and the restless air, turning together, as they have for millions of years. The weather is never just weather. It is the whole sky, alive.

image.note: A child watching the living sky, understanding it now

pages.text: Words to know. Weather: what the air is doing now. Climate: the usual weather of a place over many years. Water cycle: the endless journey of water from sea to sky and back. Atmosphere: the blanket of air around the earth. Wind: moving air.

image.note: Labelled diagram of the water cycle

pages.text: The same Sun and water that make our weather have shaped every desert, forest, and frozen pole on earth. From the wettest rainforest to the driest sand, climate makes each place what it is. Which corner of our weathered world will you explore next?
